newsitem.title: India: India, Bangladesh agree on Ganges water.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh agree on Ganges water.

text.p: India and Bangladesh reached agreement on Wednesday on sharing Ganges River water, which has vexed relations between the two nations for years.

"I wish to place on record my profound satisfaction at the agreement we have just reached on the sharing of the Ganga waters," Indian Prime Minister H. D. Deve Gowda said at a banquet for Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina.
"Without exaggeration we can say that we are opening a new chapter in Indo-Bangladesh relations (and) are also setting an example of cooperation and understanding," Deve Gowda added.
Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said she hoped the agreement would be a first step towards solving other problems that dog relations between the two countries.
"Let this agreement on the sharing of the Ganges waters be a stepping stone for greater cooperation between Bangladesh and India," Hasina said. "We want to resolve this vexed issue once and for all."
Agreement on sharing disputed Ganges water, crucial to the economies of both India and Bangladesh, is considered a major political test for Hasina.

The agreement is to be signed on Thursday, at the end of Hasina's three-day visit. Delegations from both sides met to hammer out the details after the two prime ministers held a half hour private meeting, officials said.
No details of the pact were immediately available.
The Ganges river flows through northern India before emptying into the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh.
Dhaka says India holds back water during the annual January-June dry season and releases excessive quantities during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
An agreement in 1977 to guarantee a minimum amount of water released from India was dropped five years later.
Hasina's Awami League party regained power in elections this year, 21 years after her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was assassinated in a bloody military coup.
Rahman became Bangladesh's first president after the Indian army fought a war with Pakistan which led to East Pakistan breaking away to become Bangladesh in 1971.
Hasina met Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral in the Presidential Palace after being received by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
She later met former Foreign Minister Pranab Mukherjee and Sitaram Kesri, president of India's Congress party.

While water-sharing topped her agenda, Hasina was also expected to discuss the future of a 25-year-old friendship treaty her father signed in March 1972. The accord has been criticised as a compromise to India by Hasina's rivals.
Asked if she expected a new long-term agreement with India, Hasina said: "I think after everything is finalised, then you will see."

Hasina's party said before elections this year there was no need to renew the 1972 accord because the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), including both nations, served the purpose.

Hasina was also scheduled to meet President Shankar Dayal Sharma and Vice-President K.R. Narayanan, leader of the opposition Atal Behari Vajpayee of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), during her visit.
Hasina was accompanied by Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad and Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak.
Hasina arrived in India on Tuesday and spent her first day in the western state of Rajasthan, where she offered prayers at a Moslem saint's tomb in Ajmer city.
